doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How he learned Lester Young and Parker solos
summary: Konitz explains his method: listen, sing, play along, then write the solo down last, naming Lester and Parker solos he learned.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Did you transcribe any of Lester’s solos or learn how to sing any of those early in the game or did that come later?
Oh yeah, I mean, those were some of the first ones.
Do you remember any ones in particular?

Well I remember “Dickie’s Dream” was one of my favorites and, oh lord, one after another. “Lester Leaps In” and his clarinet playing [on] “I Want a Little Girl” I think . . . I really learned a lot of those solos, and when I reviewed them recently I realized that some of them like “Shoe Shine Boy”, I had to re-learn Charlie Parker’s “Koko”, things like that. I learned Charlie Parker’s “Don’t Blame Me” which is a masterpiece of virtuosity and more than that.
When you say “learn them” do you write them down first, transcribing, or just memorize them and learn to play them on the horn after you memorize them? What’s your method?

Just listening and enjoying them and deciding I want to know them, and then singing along with them, singing away from the record from memory, playing with the record, playing without the record, and then writing it down and checking it out.
So the writing down is the last part of the process?
Which is the reverse for a lot of people.
That makes a lot of sense.
Yeah, I think so. I think I’d better cool it for a minute.
